comments.author: m11r
comments.story: Netflix and FreeBSD: Using Open Source to Deliver Streaming Video [pdf]
comments.why: Netflix's reasons ZFS benefits do not apply to CDN boxes
comments.text: Pretty sure it's still UFS+J. They've mentioned in the past that the benefits of ZFS don't really apply to the CDN boxes: if a drive dies, it's simply removed from the local cache, and files are re-downloaded/redistributed as necessary across the remaining cache drives the next time the appliance refreshes from its upstream origin. Additionally, ZFS prefetching was actually less performant in some cases from what I remember -- or at least providing no benefit -- because of how it couldn't really anticipate the I/O patterns of video segment requests from users. Additional reference: - [LINK] ("…but caching is futile.") - [VIDEO]

comments.author: toomanythings2
comments.why: Evidence Netflix delivers streaming via FreeBSD
comments.text: Netflix delivers all video streaming content via FreeBSD which makes up 37% of all internet traffic. [LINK] They also contribute to FreeBSD core. It is not just an "appliance" as some people seem to want to point to. [LINK] [LINK] [VIDEO] In addition, a guy I met, who worked at Yahoo, told me about 25% of Yahoo still runs FreeBSD as of two years ago.

comments.author: runlevel1
comments.why: Netflix talk on serving streams from FreeBSD appliances with UFS
comments.text: > I'm assuming whatever file system is on the disks... Netflix uses UFS+J on FreeBSD 10. Here are some notes from their talk at NYCBSDCon 2014: - 400,000 stream files per appliance. - 5,000 - 25,000 client streams per appliance. - 300 - 500 streams coming off each disk all the time. - Attempt to buffer 1MB ahead, but caching is futile. - Result is completely random disk workload. - System becomes limited by disk latency and CPU load. Video here: [VIDEO]
